summary: Gathers information relevant to the development of interfaces between the telephone network and the Internet, in the PINT working group's early work. It describes implementations before the formal protocol work. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2458 collects the ways people had already found to make the web and the telephone network work together, before any standard existed for it. The picture is a gateway that takes a request from the internet, hands it to the telephone network, and lets the network carry the actual call.

questions: how did the pstn and internet first interwork
how do click to dial back services work
subtitle: What the telephone and the Internet looked like when they were first wired together

tldr.problem: A web page could not ask the telephone network to do anything, and the telephone network had no way to be asked. The PINT working group set out to define interfaces that would let an Internet application request and enrich a plain old telephone service.
tldr.mechanism: The memo records four services, the common architecture the early implementations shared, and the two families of solution: one that goes through the telephone network's Intelligent Network machinery, and one that talks to the switches directly.
tldr.outcome: It is a survey of what had already been built, and it draws out the security requirements the new interfaces would have to meet. Its conclusion is that the independent implementations did not interoperate, so the working group's task was to define interfaces that would.

today: RFC 2458 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a record of what had been built before the PINT interfaces were defined, and it ends by naming the interoperability problem the working group still had to solve.

sections.title: What the Memo Is For
sections.content:
The memo gathers the information relevant to the inter-networking interfaces being developed in the Public Switched Telephone Network and Internet Inter-Networking working group. It addresses technologies, architectures and several, but by no means all, of the existing pre-PINT implementations of the arrangements through which Internet applications can request and enrich PSTN telecommunications services.

The common denominator of these enriched services, called PINT services, is that they combine the Internet and the PSTN in such a way that the Internet is used for the non-voice interactions, while the voice and fax are carried entirely over the telephone network. The memo points out that the word click should not be taken literally: it points out that initiation of the related services takes place on the Internet, where point and click are the most prevalent user actions. A service request could therefore originate from any type of IP-based platform, and there is no implication that the services must be implemented by a device within the PSTN or an Internet server running a web server.

The benefits of using the telephone network are high voice quality, the ability to route a call to different locations depending on preset criteria such as the time of day, the day of the week and geographic location, outstanding security and reliability, and access to flexible, low cost and secure billing and charging systems. The benefits of using the Internet are the uniform, well-defined and widely used interfaces available anywhere, any time.

The memo's own structure follows the same idea. It gives the basic terminology and a short description of the PINT services, then an architectural overview common to all present solutions, and then divides into two streams: one for solutions built on the Intelligent Network, and one for alternative approaches such as the CallBroker and computer-telephony integration. It then looks at the emerging standards, in particular SIP, and finishes with the overall security considerations, a conclusion, an appendix that is a tutorial on the PSTN, the Intelligent Network and call centre functions, and the references.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule that shaped every one of these systems is simple: the internet carries the request and the telephone network carries the voice. That split is why the telephone network's own strengths, its voice quality, its routing rules and its billing systems, could be kept while gaining the reach of the web.

sections.title: The Four PINT Services
sections.content:
The memo addresses four services that the working group had identified and that the pre-PINT implementations supported: click-to-dial-back, click-to-fax, click-to-fax-back and voice-access-to-content.

With click-to-dial-back, a user asks through an IP host that a telephone call be established between another party and the user. An important prerequisite is that the user has simultaneous access to both the telephone network and the Internet. One example is online shopping: a user browsing an online catalogue clicks a button, inviting a call from a sales representative. As with the all-PSTN Free-Phone or 800 service, flexible billing arrangements can be implemented on behalf of the service provider, and the telephone network can route the call depending on the time of day, the day of the week and the availability of agents in different locations.

With click-to-fax, a user at an IP host asks for a fax to be sent to a particular number. The memo argues this is especially meaningful when the fax is going to someone who has only a fax machine and no access to the Internet. The example is a web user booking a hotel room in Beijing from a travel page: the hotel has a fax machine but no Internet connection, so the user fills in the reservation form, clicks a button, and the travel service provider turns the request into a fax request and sends it with the form to the telephone network, which translates the data into the proper facsimile format and delivers it to the hotel.

Click-to-fax-back is the reverse: the user asks for a fax to be sent to them. The same example applies, with the user now requesting the hotel's confirmation, and it is also useful when the information is too large to download over the Internet without a long wait and a lot of disk space.

Voice-access-to-content asks for information on the Internet to be accessed and delivered in audio form over the telephone, using the telephone as an informational appliance. One application is to provide web access to blind people, which may need special resources available in the PSTN to convert the web data into speech.
sections.plainLanguage: Four things you could do: ask a shop to ring you back, send a form to a fax machine, have the reply faxed to you, or have a web page read aloud to you down the phone. In each case the web starts the process and the telephone network does the talking.

sections.title: The Common Architecture
sections.content:
All of the pre-PINT systems reported in the memo, those developed by AT&T, Lucent, Siemens and Nortel, vary in detail but share an architecture. In each case the service is split in two: a part for the request and a part for the execution of the service. A PINT gateway, the PSTN node that interacts with the Internet, receives the request from the Internet and passes it to the telephone network's own machinery, which carries out the service. The execution phase is identical from the telephone network's point of view in every case: the service node appears to initiate two independent calls out to the two telephones involved.

The difference between the systems lies in the language used for specifying the service. In the Intelligent Network method, the request is delivered from an Internet node, via the PINT gateway, to a Service Node over a private link, rather than by dialling from the telephone as in the pure Intelligent Network case. The effect is the same, in that the request for service is specified, although the actual parameters used may differ somewhat. The alternative systems developed by AT&T and Nortel allow the PINT gateway not to connect to the telephone network through a Service Node or other Intelligent Network component, but to connect directly to central offices that support the actions the gateway requests. The commands are then couched at a lower level, specifying the call states required for the intended service connection rather than the service identifier and the addresses involved, leaving the Intelligent Network components out of the loop. In that way the vocabulary of the commands is closer to the vocabulary used to control central offices.

The memo then sets out the interfaces that any such arrangement needs, nine of them, each with a stated purpose. Interface A is over which Internet requests for service are delivered to the Service Node; B is over which service management requests are sent from the Internet to the Service Management System; C is over which the Service Node sends call control requests to a connected central office; D is over which the Service Management System manages the Service Node; E is over which Internet requests for service are delivered to the Service Control Point; F is over which the Service Control Point sends service call control requests to the Mobile Switching Center; G is over which it sends them to the Service Switching Point; H is over which the Service Management System manages the Service Control Point; and I is over which the Service Node sends service call control requests to the Mobile Switching Center.

In practice several of these interfaces serve similar purposes, differing in whether they reflect access arrangements or a core signalling relationship. Interfaces A and E are similar, and one of the main aims of the PINT work is to ensure that they are the same. Interfaces D and H imply similar actions and are likely to carry similar messages. Interfaces C, F, G and I are all used to request that a call be initiated. The interfaces can also be viewed by the kind of components involved and the bodies that codify them: interfaces A, B and E are all to be realized as Internet protocols, while all of the others use existing protocols in the PSTN and Intelligent Network. Traditionally these have been codified by different groups, and the memo expects that to be the case in the PINT work as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Every implementation had the same shape: a request arrives over the internet, a gateway passes it into the telephone network, and the telephone network does the work. The systems differed in the vocabulary they used to describe the request, and whether they leaned on the telephone network's own service infrastructure or spoke to its switches more directly.

sections.title: What the Implementations Taught
sections.content:
The memo describes in detail the Lucent system, which separates a web server, a service node and a service management system, with a scenario for click-to-dial-back and interfaces between the web server and the service node and between the web server and the service management system, the latter managed with an SNMP MIB. It then describes the Siemens Web Call Center, where the service is delivered as a sequence of web form transactions rather than as a sequence of telephone prompts, and sets out the lessons derived from it.

Those lessons are instructive. Security was seen as a major issue: a firewall was used to control access to the Intelligent Network components, and SSL was used for communication with the agents so that the cookie values they sent with their requests were protected. For services where the entity the request appears to come from will be charged, the service has to be authorised in a way that ensures non-repudiation, which the memo suggests will mean a certificate of identity from the person making the request, tied to a financial account that the person holds with the service provider, and stored as part of the billing record.

The move from a pure Intelligent Network system to one supporting requests over the Internet changed how clients interacted with the services, so the service logic had to be redesigned. Maintaining the state of a service during its processing turned out to be a problem, and it was side-stepped by re-engineering the services as form processors, so that they dealt with fully specified requests as a single web transaction. A normal web server delivered the forms to the users, which is a change from the Intelligent Network system, where the equivalent of the prompts were sent in sequence as part of the same service process. The call centre features suited that change, but the memo is careful that this may not be true of other Intelligent Network services: it is quite common for a service to be designed so that the user is prompted and the service continues depending on the response, and a web form presents all the options at once, so that kind of prompt and collect sequence is not possible. From this it is difficult to see how an Intelligent Network service could be reused without some modification. An intermediate gateway system was provided to cocoon the service logic from the details of the components it worked with, translating calls into commands that operated with the Internet and the web server. The experience was that a service control point could be spoofed into thinking it was operating with other Intelligent Network components in the normal way, which within the limits of the service used proved simpler than originally expected.
sections.plainLanguage: The hard part was not the telephone side but the web side. A telephone service asks a question and waits for the answer; a web page asks everything at once and waits for the whole form. The memo describes how one team rebuilt its telephone services to suit that, and what it cost.

sections.title: SIP as the Emerging Standard
sections.content:
The memo singles out SIP, the Session Initiation Protocol, as a promising solution to the PINT problem. SIP was then under development in the IETF working group for multiparty multimedia session control, and provides call forwarding including the equivalent of 700-, 800- and 900-type calls, call forwarding on no answer, on busy and unconditionally, other address translation services, delivery of calling and called numbers in any naming scheme, personal mobility so a party can be reached at one location-independent address even when the user changes terminals, negotiation of how to reach a party, caller and callee authentication, blind and supervised call transfer, user location, and invitation to multicast conferences. Extensions for third-party signalling, for click-to-dial-back services, for fully meshed conferences and for connections to Multipoint Control Units, as well as mixed modes and the transition between them, had been specified.

SIP addresses are URLs and can be embedded in web pages. It is addressing-neutral, with addresses expressed as URLs of various types such as SIP, H.323 or telephone. The memo gives a purely representational example of a SIP URL, sip:+12125551212@foo.example.com, where foo.example.com is the host serving as a gateway into the PSTN. SIP is independent of the packet layer and needs only an unreliable datagram service, because it provides its own reliability mechanism; while it is typically used over UDP or TCP, the memo observes that it could run over IPX, or carrier pigeons, ATM AAL5 or X.25, in rough order of desirability. It can also set up calls out of band: the signalling exchange uses IP, but the actual data transport can take place over the PSTN, which makes it possible to use SIP to control a PBX or to send requests to a Service Control Point. The PINT services make use of that flexibility.

The protocol itself is textual and client-server, similar in syntax to HTTP and RTSP. A request carries a method, which is INVITE, BYE, ACK or REGISTER, a list of parameter-value pairs describing the request and an optional body. Parameters include the origin and destination of the call and a unique call identifier, and may indicate the caller's organisation along with the call's subject and priority. The body describes the call to be established or the conference to be joined; the format is not prescribed by SIP, and SDP was one possibility being standardized, with an additional phone number address format to be added to SDP for the purposes of the PINT services. Responses say whether a request is still being processed, was successful, could possibly be satisfied by another node, or failed; a redirect response names the node to try next, and an unsuccessful call may also return a better time to try again. In a typical successful call the caller sends an INVITE, the callee accepts by returning a response code, and the caller confirms with an ACK. Either side can end the call with a BYE. Requests can be authenticated using standard HTTP password and challenge-response mechanisms, and requests and responses may also be signed and encrypted.

SIP distinguishes three kinds of entities. User agents receive and initiate calls and may forward them. A proxy server is an intermediary that acts as both a server and a client, servicing requests internally or passing them on, possibly after translation, and must interpret and if necessary rewrite a request before forwarding it. A redirect server accepts a request, maps the address into zero or more new addresses and returns them to the client; unlike a proxy it does not initiate its own request, and unlike a user agent server it does not accept calls. Proxy and redirect servers may use location servers that determine the current likely location of the callee. A PSTN gateway initiates phone calls between two parties, either as a server that sends requests to a Service Control Point or as a computer-telephony-controlled PBX. The servers that control a PBX or a Service Control Point act as user agents, and a web server may also act as a SIP user agent.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP is a web-style protocol for setting up calls. It looks like HTTP, it carries addresses as web addresses, and it can start a call in the telephone network while the conversation itself stays there. The memo thinks this is the elegant answer to the problem the working group was set up to solve.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Conclusion
sections.content:
Inter-networking the Internet and the PSTN means introducing new interfaces, such as A, B and E in the memo's diagram, and to make sure their use does not put the networks, and in particular the PSTN, at additional risk, those interfaces have to be designed with proper security considerations. Two of the pre-PINT implementations, the Lucent and the Siemens systems, handled the security aspect, and their experience suggests four requirements.

Peer entity authentication, so that a communicating entity can prove its identity to another in the network, for example the requesting IP host to the PINT gateway and the PINT gateway to the PSTN node providing the service control function. Authorization and access control, to verify whether a network entity is allowed to use a network resource, for example whether a requesting IP host may ask the PINT gateway for services. Non-repudiation, to account for all operations in case of doubt or dispute. And confidentiality, to avoid disclosure of information such as an end user's profile information and data without the permission of its owner. The memo expects that further requirements will arise as the PINT interfaces are developed, and says it is imperative that the resulting interfaces include specific means to meet all of the security requirements.

The conclusion is that the memo has provided the information relevant to developing inter-networking interfaces between the PSTN and the Internet for the PINT services, covering technologies, architectures and several existing pre-PINT implementations of the arrangements through which Internet applications can request and enrich PSTN telecommunications services. The key observation is that the pre-PINT implementations, having been developed independently, do not interoperate. It is the task of the PINT working group to define the inter-networking interfaces that will support inter-operation of the future implementations of PINT services.
sections.plainLanguage: Joining two networks means new doors between them, and each door needs a lock, a list of who is allowed through, a record of what was done, and protection of what travels through. The memo lists those four needs and then makes its point: the systems built so far do not talk to each other, which is the problem the working group exists to solve.

items.title: Peer entity authentication
items.text: So that one end of a new interface can prove who it is to the other, such as an IP host to the PINT gateway.

items.title: Authorization and access control
items.text: So that a network entity can be checked for permission to use a resource, such as asking the gateway for a service.

items.title: Non-repudiation
items.text: So that every operation can be accounted for in case of doubt or dispute.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: So that a user's profile information and data are not disclosed without the owner's permission.
